nodes.title: Amazon S3: Key Ideas
nodes.content: S3 is AWS's object store — flat namespace of buckets containing objects, accessed via HTTP. It backs almost every AWS architecture: data lakes, static sites, backups, lambda triggers, CloudFront origins. The exam tests storage classes, encryption, access control, and event notifications.

flashcards.front: S3 storage classes — pick one for backups, one for hot data, one for archive.
flashcards.back: Hot: S3 Standard (high cost, instant access). Backups / infrequent: S3 Standard-IA (cheaper storage, retrieval fee). Archive: Glacier Deep Archive (cheapest storage, retrieval in hours). Lifecycle policies move objects between classes automatically based on age.

flashcards.front: S3 bucket policy vs IAM policy vs ACL — which to use?
flashcards.back: IAM policy: 'this user/role can read bucket X'. Bucket policy: 'these principals can access this bucket' — required for cross-account and public access. ACL (legacy): per-object permissions, mostly avoided today. Use bucket policies for most cross-account, IAM for in-account.

flashcards.front: How do you make an S3 website (static-site hosting)?
flashcards.back: Enable static-website hosting on the bucket, upload index.html, set a bucket policy allowing public-read on objects, point a CloudFront distribution at it for HTTPS + edge caching. Don't expose the bucket directly — CloudFront with an OAC (Origin Access Control) is the canonical pattern.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between server-side and client-side encryption?
flashcards.back: SSE: data encrypted by S3 after upload. Variants: SSE-S3 (AWS-managed key, easiest), SSE-KMS (your KMS key, audit trail), SSE-C (you supply the key on each request). Client-side: you encrypt before upload — S3 only sees ciphertext. Pick SSE-KMS for compliance, SSE-S3 for default-on.

questions.q: A security engineer needs to ensure all data stored in an S3 bucket is encrypted with a specific CMK, and any PutObject request without SSE-KMS using that key is rejected. How should the bucket policy be written?
choices: Enable default bucket encryption with SSE-KMS and the CMK and rely on it to reject any non-KMS uploads automatically
Write a KMS key policy that allows the Encrypt action only when the request originates from that specific S3 bucket
Write a bucket policy that allows all s3:PutObject calls and let KMS enforce that the data was encrypted properly
Write a bucket policy that Denies s3:PutObject when s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption is not 'aws:kms' OR the kms-key-id header is not the specific CMK ARN
questions.explanation: Default encryption applies SSE-KMS if no header is provided but does not reject a PutObject that explicitly specifies a different algorithm or key, so an explicit-Deny bucket policy on the two relevant request headers is required for strict enforcement. KMS key policies authorise key use but don't reject S3 uploads that bypass KMS. Allowing all PutObject and 'trusting KMS' doesn't enforce the algorithm header at all. The bucket policy is the right control because that's where the request headers can be evaluated.

questions.q: A developer needs read access to an S3 bucket in Account B from an EC2 instance in Account A. The bucket policy in Account B already grants s3:GetObject to Account A's EC2 role ARN. However, the GetObject calls are still failing. What is the MOST likely missing configuration?
choices: Versioning must be enabled on the bucket in Account B because cross-account reads require object versioning to expose object metadata
The EC2 instance's IAM role in Account A must have an identity-based policy allowing s3:GetObject on the specific bucket ARN in Account B
Account A must create a VPC endpoint for S3 to enable any cross-account bucket access from instances inside the VPC
Account B must accept a VPC peering connection from Account A's VPC before S3 cross-account requests will succeed
questions.explanation: Cross-account S3 access requires Allow from BOTH sides — the bucket policy in Account B AND an identity-based policy on the IAM role in Account A; granting only the bucket policy is the most common mistake. S3 has no dependency on versioning for cross-account reads. A VPC endpoint changes the network path but isn't required for cross-account access. VPC peering is irrelevant — S3 traffic doesn't traverse VPC peering.

questions.q: A company needs to enforce that all S3 buckets created in their accounts use SSE-KMS encryption and have public access blocked. New accounts joining the organization must automatically comply. Which combination achieves this with ZERO manual per-account configuration?
choices: Deploy Lambda functions per account triggered by S3 bucket creation events to enforce the encryption and public-access settings after the fact across the organisation
Use an SCP denying s3:CreateBucket without SSE-KMS, plus organisation-level S3 Block Public Access, plus a Config conformance pack via StackSets with auto-deployment
Create a CloudFormation StackSet that deploys a baseline S3 bucket policy template to every existing account and re-applies the template whenever a new bucket is created
Use AWS Control Tower detective guardrails to flag S3 buckets without encryption or with public access enabled and rely on the SecOps team to remediate each finding manually
questions.explanation: The zero-touch enforcement combination is: an SCP that denies bucket creation without SSE-KMS headers, organisation-level S3 Block Public Access for all accounts (current and future), and a conformance pack deployed via StackSets with auto-deployment for new accounts. Per-account Lambda after the fact is reactive. A StackSet that 'deploys bucket policies on creation' isn't natively triggered by bucket events. Detective guardrails report after the fact and require manual remediation.

questions.q: A bucket policy denies all requests where aws:SecureTransport is false. Which TWO additional controls would you add to BLOCK accidental public exposure of objects in this bucket?
choices: Enable S3 Block Public Access at the bucket level to override any policy or ACL that would grant public read
Enable default S3 server-side encryption with SSE-S3 so newly uploaded objects are encrypted at rest by default
Enable S3 Object Ownership set to 'Bucket owner enforced' so ACLs are disabled and uploaders cannot grant public access on individual objects
Enable versioning with MFA Delete so deletion of object versions requires an MFA-authenticated root call
questions.explanation: Block Public Access overrides any bucket policy or ACL that would grant public access, and 'Bucket owner enforced' Object Ownership disables ACLs entirely so per-object ACL grants can no longer make individual objects public. SSE-S3 protects data at rest but doesn't gate access — public reads of encrypted objects are still served decrypted to authorised callers. MFA Delete protects against accidental version deletion, not against public reads.

correct.useCase: Create and control encryption keys (CMKs) with automatic rotation, key policies, and CloudTrail audit of every use.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.

questions.q: A CloudTrail data event is required to log all S3 GetObject API calls on a specific bucket containing PII data. The security team also wants to detect when someone downloads more than 1,000 objects in a 5-minute window. Which combination achieves both requirements?
choices: Configure Amazon Macie to monitor GetObject API calls and alert on high-volume download patterns from a single principal
Enable S3 Event Notifications for GetObject events into SNS, then use CloudWatch Metric Math to count the messages
Enable S3 server access logging to a target bucket and have a Lambda function parse the log files to count GetObject calls
Enable CloudTrail data events for the S3 bucket sending to CloudWatch Logs, create a metric filter on GetObject and alarm when the count exceeds 1,000 in 5 minutes
questions.explanation: S3 object-level operations (GetObject/PutObject) are CloudTrail data events, off by default; enabling them for the bucket, streaming to CloudWatch Logs and adding a metric filter + alarm gives you a managed, near-real-time counter for the threshold. Macie detects sensitive data and unusual S3 access patterns but isn't a configurable per-bucket GetObject counter. S3 Event Notifications fire on object events but not on GetObject and can't be sized into 5-minute windows trivially. S3 server access logs have delivery delay and gaps and aren't suitable for real-time threshold alarms.

questions.q: A company uses AWS Organizations with 20 accounts. Each account must have CloudTrail enabled with logs sent to a central S3 bucket in the security account. Account administrators should NOT be able to disable CloudTrail or modify the trail. Which configuration achieves this?
choices: Deploy an EventBridge rule per account that detects CloudTrail StopLogging events and automatically re-enables the trail via a Lambda
Create an organization trail from the management account so it applies to all current and future member accounts and cannot be disabled by them
Use CloudFormation StackSets to deploy per-account trails and add an SCP that denies cloudtrail:StopLogging and cloudtrail:DeleteTrail
Enable the AWS Config managed rule 'cloud-trail-enabled' in every account with auto-remediation that recreates the trail if it gets disabled
questions.explanation: An organisation trail created from the management account propagates to every member account, AWS prevents member admins from disabling, modifying or deleting it, and all events are centralised in one S3 bucket — the simplest authoritative control. EventBridge-and-Lambda is reactive (a window of disabled logging always exists). StackSets + SCP works but is more moving parts than the single organisation-trail mechanism. A Config managed rule with auto-remediation is also reactive and per-account.

questions.q: A company is implementing a data lake on S3. The data governance team requires that all data queries and who accessed which datasets be audited for HIPAA compliance. Which S3 logging mechanism provides the most detailed per-request audit trail including the requester's identity?
choices: Amazon Macie running on the data lake buckets to classify sensitive data and surface access patterns by user activity
S3 server access logging delivered to a target bucket, capturing requester, bucket, key, action and status code for each request
CloudTrail S3 data events, recording every GetObject/PutObject/DeleteObject with the IAM principal ARN, account ID, source IP and object key
VPC Flow Logs on the subnets that host workloads, capturing network traffic to/from the S3 VPC endpoint for after-the-fact correlation
questions.explanation: CloudTrail S3 data events give the strongest audit trail for HIPAA: the IAM principal ARN, account, source IP, object key, action and timestamp for every object-level request, with log file integrity validation and centralised aggregation across accounts. Macie classifies data but isn't a per-request audit log. S3 server access logs can have delivery delay and don't always include the full IAM principal ARN. VPC Flow Logs see network 5-tuples, not the IAM identity or object key.

questions.q: A company wants to restrict all AWS API calls to originate only from the company's corporate IP range (203.0.113.0/24). All other API calls from any source should be denied. Where should this restriction be applied for the STRONGEST enforcement?
choices: Add an IAM permission boundary to all IAM users requiring an aws:SourceIp condition on every API call
Enable AWS CloudTrail and have EventBridge real-time rules detect API calls from unknown IPs and trigger Lambda revocation
Configure an identity-based IAM policy on each IAM user and role that denies access when aws:SourceIp is outside the corporate range
Create a Service Control Policy at the organization root with Deny on all actions when aws:SourceIp is not in 203.0.113.0/24 (with an aws:ViaAWSService exception)
questions.explanation: An SCP at the organisation root is the strongest control because it applies to every principal in every member account — including account-level admins and root users — and cannot be overridden by lower-level IAM policies. Permission boundaries only constrain individual IAM entities and don't apply to root users. EventBridge-on-CloudTrail is detective and reactive, not preventive. Per-identity policies must be replicated to every principal and can be undone by any account admin.

questions.q: A company requires that all API calls to AWS are made only through approved network paths (corporate network or VPN). An SCP should deny any API call not originating from the approved IP ranges (203.0.113.0/24 and 198.51.100.0/24). Which SCP condition correctly implements this?
choices: Deny '*' with NotIpAddress on aws:SourceIp = [the two approved ranges] plus a Null check on aws:ViaAWSService to skip AWS service calls
Allow '*' with IpAddress on aws:SourceIp restricted to [203.0.113.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24] so only those source addresses are ever permitted by the policy
Deny '*' with IpAddress on aws:SourceIp = [203.0.113.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24] so calls from inside the listed corporate ranges are blocked instead
Deny '*' with StringNotEquals on aws:SourceVpc set to a specific VPC ID to restrict the entire organisation to traffic from that single VPC
questions.explanation: The right pattern uses NotIpAddress (deny when source IP is NOT in the approved set) combined with a Null check on aws:ViaAWSService so AWS-internal service-to-service calls (CloudFormation→EC2, Lambda→S3) aren't blocked by the user-IP check. An Allow-only SCP is wrong because SCPs control deny semantics on top of identity Allows. IpAddress (option C) would deny the approved ranges — the opposite of intent. aws:SourceVpc restricts by VPC, not by corporate IP range.

questions.q: A company wants to prevent developers from disabling GuardDuty, Security Hub, or Config in any account in their AWS Organization. What is the MOST effective way to enforce this?
choices: Enable AWS Config managed rules that detect when these services are disabled and trigger an SNS notification to the security team for manual response
Apply SCPs at the organization root or OU level that deny guardduty:DeleteDetector, securityhub:DisableSecurityHub and config:StopConfigurationRecorder for all accounts
Attach IAM permission boundaries to every IAM user in member accounts that deny the disable-actions for those three services across the organisation
Configure EventBridge rules in each account to detect disable events and trigger Lambda functions that re-enable the services automatically
questions.explanation: Only an SCP at the organisation root or OU level is a true preventive control across every principal in every member account — including account-level admins and root users — so the disable APIs simply fail. Config-rule notifications and EventBridge-driven re-enabling are detective and reactive (a window of disabled state always exists). Permission boundaries only constrain individual IAM entities they are attached to and don't apply to root users; they're not an organisation-wide control.

questions.q: An application's Lambda function needs to call an external SaaS API that requires basic authentication. The API credentials should be securely stored, automatically rotated every 30 days, and NOT appear in environment variables or code. Which service provides this with the LEAST operational overhead?
choices: KMS-encrypt the credentials and bake the ciphertext into the Lambda deployment package, decrypting at runtime
Store the credentials in an S3 object encrypted with KMS and have Lambda fetch and decrypt them on every invocation
Store the credentials in AWS Secrets Manager with a rotation Lambda configured for a 30-day schedule, calling GetSecretValue at runtime
Store the credentials in SSM Parameter Store SecureString and retrieve them via the SSM GetParameter API at runtime
questions.explanation: Secrets Manager natively supports scheduled rotation via a Lambda rotation function — for a SaaS credential you write a small rotator that creates the new credential at the SaaS side and updates the secret on the configured cadence; the function calls GetSecretValue without env vars. Baking ciphertext into the deployment package or fetching from S3 each call works but adds custom code and isn't natively rotatable. SSM Parameter Store SecureString lacks native automatic rotation — you'd have to build it yourself.

questions.q: A company has a Lambda function that needs to access a Secrets Manager secret. The function is deployed in multiple accounts. What is the MOST efficient way to share the secret across accounts while maintaining encryption?
choices: Store the secret in SSM Parameter Store with a cross-account resource policy and have each Lambda fetch it from the central account
Create an IAM role in the secret's account that each remote Lambda execution role can assume, then call GetSecretValue once assumed
Export the secret value via a deployment pipeline and store a copy in each account's own Secrets Manager
Add a Secrets Manager resource policy to the secret allowing the other accounts' Lambda execution roles to call GetSecretValue, and grant kms:Decrypt on the CMK to those same roles
questions.explanation: Secrets Manager supports a resource-based policy on the secret; granting cross-account Lambda execution roles GetSecretValue plus kms:Decrypt on the encrypting CMK lets the remote Lambdas read directly without role assumption hops. SSM Parameter Store can do cross-account but lacks Secrets Manager rotation features. Role assumption works but adds latency and is more code than the direct resource-policy approach. Copying secrets per account multiplies the surface area and rotation problem.

nodes.title: Automate threat response

data.scenario: Detect a threat and respond without a human in the loop. Order the AWS services.

nodes.explanation: GuardDuty raises a finding, an EventBridge rule matches it and triggers a Lambda that remediates the issue and then publishes an SNS alert to notify responders.
